description: Relations and facts on 20 September 1378 whose source is a western European realm, from research/europe-west.md. obedience: the Pope each Catholic realm follows in the Western Schism on the start day (plan-1378 4.4); null means it has not chosen yet.

relations.explanation: Richard II is Lord of Ireland; James Butler, Earl of Ormond, governs as justiciar until Edmund Mortimer arrives as lieutenant (1379).
William Montagu, Earl of Salisbury, holds Man of the English crown (sold to William le Scrope in 1392).
Calais, coastal Gascony, and the leased fortresses of Brest (1378-97) and Cherbourg (1378-94) under the Captain of Calais and the Seneschal of Gascony.
Butler earldom of Kilkenny and Tipperary; the earl is also the king's justiciar.
FitzGerald earldom of Kerry and Limerick, largely independent and Gaelicised under Gearóid Iarla.
Pale earldom of Maynooth, loyal to the colony's government.
Lesser Munster lords render dues to the Earl of Desmond.
John of Islay submitted to David II in 1369 and is Robert II's son-in-law; a semi-royal Gaelic lordship.
William, 1st Earl of Douglas and Mar, the greatest border magnate; Galloway is held apart by Archibald the Grim.
Norwegian earldom, vacant on the start day under a royal captain; Henry Sinclair is invested at Marstrand on 2 Aug 1379.
Philip the Bold holds the duchy as an apanage and peerage; heir by marriage to Flanders, Artois, Nevers, Rethel and the County of Burgundy.
Louis I, the king's eldest brother, holds Anjou, Maine and Touraine and is lieutenant in Languedoc.
John of Berry holds Berry and Auvergne, with Poitou since its reconquest (1372).
Peerage duchy of Louis II, the dauphin's maternal uncle.
Valois-Alençon county of Peter II, with Perche.
On the French side since its appeal against the Black Prince (1368); its lands border English Gascony.
Foix is held of the crown, but Gaston Fébus holds Béarn 'of God alone' and keeps a careful neutrality.
Arnaud-Amanieu VIII went over to France in 1368 and married the queen's sister Margaret of Bourbon.
Homage disputed; John IV has been in English exile since 1373, royal garrisons hold much of the duchy, and Charles V's court confiscates it in Dec 1378.
The heir's principality, held by the nine-year-old dauphin Charles and run by a royal governor.
Margaret of France holds Artois of the crown (and the County of Burgundy of the Empire) until her death on 9 May 1382.
Vendôme, Eu, La Marche, Comminges, Penthièvre, Laval, Valentinois and other lesser fiefs of the crown.
Joanna I of Naples is Countess of Provence and Forcalquier, governed by a seneschal at Aix.
Papal Comtat and Avignon under rectors and the cardinals left behind; it goes over to Clement VII in the autumn.
The Caroline war: the Truce of Bruges expired in June 1377; French raids on the English coast and Gaunt's failed siege of Saint-Malo (Aug-Sep 1378) follow.
Richard II holds Edward III's claim to the French crown and the remnants of Aquitaine that Charles V's reconquest left.

historical_end.how: War resumed on the March; Lochmaben taken by the Scots (1384).

relations.explanation: Fourteen-year truce of 1369, with constant raiding on the March; the Scots seize Berwick castle briefly in Nov 1378.
Scotland claims Berwick, Roxburgh, Jedburgh, Lochmaben and Annandale, still in English hands.

historical_end.how: Treaty of Bayonne: Gaunt gave up his claim for a marriage and a pension.

relations.explanation: Castile is France's naval ally and its galleys raid the English coast; John of Gaunt claims the Castilian throne.
Treaty of London (1373), renewed at Windsor in 1386.
Charles the Bad leases Cherbourg to England for English help; Thomas Trivet's troops go to Navarre.
John IV's treaty with Edward III; the duke lives in England and Brest is leased to the English.
The Auld Alliance, renewed by Robert II at Vincennes in 1371.
Treaty of Toledo: Castilian galleys serve France and Castile invades Navarre on France's side.

historical_end.how: Peace of Briones ended the Castilian war; France kept the seized lands until the exchange of 1404.

relations.explanation: After Jacques de Rue's confession Charles V seized Charles the Bad's Norman counties and Montpellier (Apr-Jun 1378) and holds his son; Castile fights the field war in Navarre.
Charles the Bad's long feud with the Valois over his Norman and Champagne claims.
Joan of Penthièvre and her sons keep the Blois claim to the duchy (John of Blois a captive in England until 1387).
The Béarn inheritance feud; Launac (1362) is recent, but a peace in 1377 and a marriage in 1379 settle it for a time.
Routier captains holding Ventadour, Carlat and other castles in Auvergne, the Limousin and Rouergue live by ransoms on the countryside.
Philip the Bold married Margaret of Male, heiress of Flanders, at Ghent.
Margaret of France is the mother of Louis of Male, her heir.
Niall Mór Ó Néill presses on the earldom of Ulster and Louth.
Art Mór MacMurrough Kavanagh raids the Pale and takes crown fees and black rent.
O'Connor Faly, O'More, O'Byrne and O'Toole raid the colony and draw black rent.
O'Donnell and O'Neill contest the supremacy of Ulster.
FitzGerald and O'Brien contest the supremacy of Munster.
The Burkes against the O'Connor kingship of Connacht (one kingship under Ruaidrí until the split of 1384).

historical_end.how: Peace of Briones; Castile holds Navarrese fortresses as pledges.

relations.explanation: The Infante John invades Navarre and besieges Pamplona after Charles II's dealings with England.
Wary peace after the War of the Two Peters, sealed at Almazán (1375).

historical_end.how: Ferdinand reopened war with English help (third Fernandine war, 1381-82).

relations.explanation: Treaty of Santarém ended the second Fernandine war.
Muhammad V keeps peace with Henry II through renewed truces; no regular tribute found.

historical_end.how: Abu al-Abbas lost and regained the throne; Granadan control lapsed.

relations.explanation: Granada raises and controls the Marinid sultan Abu al-Abbas Ahmad at Fez and received Gibraltar from him.
Sardinia, Corsica and the western Mediterranean trade.

historical_end.how: Peace made by Eleanor of Arborea (renewed war 1391).

relations.explanation: Arborea's war to drive the Crown of Aragon from Sardinia; Hugh III holds most of the island.
The new Trastámara nobility of Henry II's grants (Enríquez, Villena, Guzmán, Manrique, Mendoza, Velasco).
Santiago, Calatrava and Alcántara.
Constituent kingdom with its Cortes and the Justicia.
Principality with its Corts and the Generalitat; the king lives here.
Constituent kingdom.
The Aragonese kingdom of Sardinia, reduced to Cagliari, Alghero and some castles.
Co-principality under the Pariatges: Gaston Fébus of Foix and the Bishop of Urgell.
War of Chioggia over Tenedos and the straits trade (battle of Antium, 30 May 1378).
The two maritime republics contest the Levant and Black Sea trade.
Francesco da Carrara joins Genoa and Hungary; fighting around Mestre and Treviso.
Carrara-Venetian enmity (wars of 1372-73 and 1378-81).

historical_end.how: Peace of Turin: Venice pays Hungary yearly and confirms Dalmatia.

relations.explanation: Louis I joins the league against Venice.
Patriarch Marquard joins the anti-Venetian league and takes Istrian towns.
League against Venice.
League against Venice.
League against Venice.
The Carrara are Hungary's allies against Venice.
Bernabò Visconti allied with Venice; attacks Genoese lands.
Peter II of Cyprus joins Venice against Genoa over Famagusta.
Bernabò, as Venice's ally, backs Genoese exiles and attacks the Riviera.
Genoa has held Famagusta since 1374.
Bernabò presses his wife Regina della Scala's claim to the Scaliger inheritance; Jacopo dal Verme serves Verona.

historical_end.how: Gian Galeazzo seized Bernabò and reunited the state.

relations.explanation: The Visconti state divided at Galeazzo II's death; Milan city held jointly; Bernabò's sons threaten Gian Galeazzo.
Gian Galeazzo's mother is Bianca of Savoy, Amadeus VI's sister.
Gian Galeazzo married Isabelle of Valois (d. 1373) and holds the county of Vertus.
Galeazzo II's troops took Asti; the 1377 marriage alliance is breaking; Secondotto blames the Visconti.
Piedmont border; Savoy-Achaea.
Savoy demands Saluzzo's homage; Frederick II swore homage to the Dauphin instead (1375).
The War of the Eight Saints has just ended (Tivoli, July 1378); distrust remains.
Tuscan rivalry (Montepulciano).
Allies in the war against the papal legates.
The Malatesta-Montefeltro feud.
The Ordelaffi retook Forlì by revolt against the Church.
Antonio da Montefeltro retook Urbino by revolt; no vicariate yet.
The Kingdom of Naples is a papal fief; Urban VI deposes Joanna in 1380.
The Este are papal vicars of Ferrara (Modena is an imperial fief).
Galeotto I Malatesta holds Rimini, Fano, Fossombrone, Pesaro and Cesena as papal vicar.
Varano papal vicariate.
The Polenta of Ravenna, the Alidosi of Imola and Hawkwood's Bagnacavallo and Cotignola.
Commune under direct papal government, with Albornoz's citadel.
Colonna, Orsini, Savelli, Caetani of Fondi and the Prefetti di Vico; the Caetani and the Prefetti back Clement.
Free commune since the 1376 revolt, under nominal papal sovereignty after the 1377 settlement.
Autonomous commune under the Raspanti since expelling the papal governor (Dec 1375); papal sovereignty not enforced.
Frederick II swore homage to the Dauphin of France against Savoy's claim.
Crown Flanders is a French peerage; Louis of Male does homage but balances France against England.
Ghent leads the Four Members of Flanders; its great revolt against the count begins in September 1379.
Hainaut is held with Holland and Zeeland by the Wittelsbachs; Albert governs it as regent for William V.
The lords of Arkel hold part of their land of the count of Holland and are independent-minded; the Arkel war comes in 1401.
The Barrois mouvant west of the Meuse is a French fief since the Treaty of Bruges (1301); Robert I is John II's son-in-law.
Vaudémont is a Lorraine fief, held by Margaret of Joinville and Peter of Geneva.
Soest is the leading town of the archbishop of Cologne's Duchy of Westphalia.
Many Schwarzburg lands are Wettin fiefs.
After the Vogtland war the Vögte and many Thuringian counts hold Wettin fiefs.
Bought by Charles IV in 1373 and joined to the Bohemian crown lands at Tangermünde (1374); assigned to his son Sigismund. It keeps its electoral vote.
William II of Jülich acts for his son William I, invested with Guelders by Charles IV in 1377.
First Guelders succession war: William of Jülich's party against Mathilda of Guelders and her husband John of Blois-Châtillon (here inside french_minor_lordships). Mathilda renounces on 24 Mar 1379.
Cleves backed Mathilda's party in Guelders (relief army at Hönnepel, 1378).
Cleves opposes a Jülich-Guelders block around it.
Baesweiler (22 Aug 1371): Jülich and Guelders defeated and captured Wenceslaus of Brabant.
Brabant holds Grave and the Meuse against Guelders since Baesweiler.
Adolf of Cleves and Engelbert III of the Mark are brothers.
Both branches of the house of Jülich.
The counts of Holland claim lordship over Frisia; invasion 1396-1401.
Border feuds over the Sticht and the Lek.
Albert is a Wittelsbach co-duke of Bavaria; the Straubing share is held with Holland.
Mainz schism: Louis of Meissen, a Wettin brother and Charles IV's and Gregory XI's choice, disputes the see with Adolf of Nassau until 1381.
Charles IV opposed Adolf of Nassau, who had stood against Wenceslaus's election.
Mainz enclaves (Fritzlar, Amöneburg) lie in Hesse; a Mainz-led coalition besieges Kassel in 1385.
Hesse-Wettin inheritance pact (Erbverbrüderung) of 1373.
The city has fought its archbishop since Worringen; the last war ended in 1377.
Princes against the city leagues; war in 1388-89.
Duke John I serves the French crown.
Metz captured Robert of Bar in 1368; border feuds.
Otto VI of Tecklenburg holds most of Osnabrück's castles.
Archbishop Peter Gelyto is Charles IV's man.
Elector Wenceslaus I and his nephew Albert hold Lüneburg for the Ascanians under the Peace of Hanover (1373).

historical_end.how: The Welfs won at Winsen an der Aller.

relations.explanation: Peace of Hanover: alternating Ascanian and Welf rule sealed by marriages; Henry of Brunswick refused it. The war flares again and ends at Winsen (28 May 1388).
Lüneburg town backs the Ascanians after expelling the Welf dukes in 1371.
Archbishop Albert II is a Welf, uncle of Magnus II's sons.
Otto the Evil holds the Brunswick lands as self-made guardian; Frederick drives him out in 1381 or 1384.
Dinklar (1367); the see and the Welfs feud over the Leine-Oker lands.
Albert II claims Denmark for his grandson Albert IV against Olaf II, chosen in 1376.
Albert II's son Albert is King of Sweden; Mecklenburg knights hold Swedish castles.
Junior Mecklenburg line.
The Rendsburg counts hold most of Schleswig by pledge during Olaf II's minority; Denmark refuses them the fief until Nyborg (1386).
Enmity since Wöhrden (1319).
Lauenburg contests the Saxon electoral vote the Golden Bull gave to Wittenberg.
The Wendish leaders guard the Lübeck-Hamburg road together.
Three-city league of Erfurt, Mühlhausen and Nordhausen.
The Hanse expelled Brunswick after the Great Schicht (1374); readmitted in 1380.
Margrave Jobst holds Moravia as a fief of the Bohemian crown (from 1375); his brothers Prokop and John Sobieslaus hold appanages inside it.

The Silesian dukes (Legnica, Brzeg, Opole, Oleśnica, Głogów-Żagań, Cieszyn, Opava-Racibórz) are vassals of the Bohemian crown since Trenčín (1335); Świdnica-Jawor is held for life by the dowager Agnes.
Crown duchy of Breslau, governed by the city for the king.
Bohemian crown land with the Six Towns League (1346); Görlitz carved out for John of Görlitz in 1377.
Bought by Charles IV in 1367 and joined to the Bohemian crown; held directly by the king, not yet pledged.
Görlitz and its district made an appanage duchy for John of Görlitz (born 1370), Charles IV's third son; back to the crown on his death (1396).
The Rosenberg (Rožmberk) brothers Jan I and Oldřich I hold the greatest magnate lordship of south Bohemia under the crown.
The counts of Cilli (Hermann I with his nephew William) hold their lands under the Habsburg dukes of Styria; princes of the Empire only in 1436.
Self-governing Habsburg town since the Kyburg inheritance (1277), with a Burgrecht with Bern.
Pledged to Habsburg by Louis the Bavarian in 1330; regains imperial status in 1415.
Valley under a Habsburg bailiff (Peter von Thorberg) since the 1355 peace undid its confederate pact; frees itself in 1387-88 (Näfels).
Prince-bishopric under Tyrolean, now Habsburg, advocacy.
Prince-bishopric bound to the Habsburg counts of Tyrol by the compacts of 1363 with Rudolf IV.
Schwyz names the Ammann of Zug since 1365; Habsburg keeps rights and revenues under the Thorberg peace; the other places force Schwyz back in 1404.
Iceland under the Norwegian crown since the Old Covenant (1262-64), with its own law (Jónsbók) and Althing, ruled through a royal governor.
Norwegian crown land with the Løgting at Tinganes; trade through Bergen.
The Eastern Settlement under the Norwegian crown since 1261; trade a royal monopoly from Bergen, but the royal ship is lost c.1367-69 and contact is lapsing.

historical_end.how: Lucerne seized Habsburg towns in winter 1385-86; Leopold III invaded and fell at Sempach.

relations.explanation: Thorberg peace between the Habsburgs and the confederates, extended in March 1376 for eleven years.
Habsburg claims rights over Lucerne, Zug and the Waldstätte countryside; the confederates take Habsburg towns whenever they can. Renounced in the twenty-year peace of 1394.
Open feud between Eberhard II and the Swabian City League since the league's victory at Reutlingen (14 May 1377); the Town War follows in 1387-89 (Döffingen, 23 Aug 1388).
Duke Frederick holds the Lower Swabian Landvogtei after the Peace of Nuremberg (Aug 1378) and presses the imperial cities; war again in 1388.
Salt trade and borders; the Bavarian dukes seize Archbishop Pilgrim II in 1387 for his league with the cities.
The Hohenzollern burgraves hold the castle and burgravial rights inside the imperial city until the city buys them out (1427).
Valdemar IV took back Scania and Gotland (1360-61); Albert of Sweden treats Gotland as Swedish and backs his nephew's claim to the Danish throne. No open war on the start day.
Haakon VI was deposed as Swedish co-king in 1364; the war against Albert (1364-71) ended in a peace that left his claim alive.
The Karelian border after Nöteborg (1323); Novgorod raids Finland and both tax the Karelians and Sámi.
Albert II of Mecklenburg claims the Danish throne for his grandson Albert IV, son of Valdemar's elder daughter Ingeborg, against Olaf.
Haakon VI married Margaret (1363); their son Olaf is King of Denmark and Haakon's heir in Norway. A personal union on Haakon's death (1380).
Albert of Sweden is the son of Duke Albert II of Mecklenburg; Mecklenburg men hold Swedish castles.
The Peace of Stralsund left the Hanse its Scanian castles for 15 years, and the Hanse backed Olaf's election against Mecklenburg (1376). They cooperate until the 1420s.
Stephen III married Taddea Visconti, Bernabò's daughter; the dukes are Visconti allies (Frederick marries Maddalena Visconti in 1381).
Wittelsbach kin; the house treaty of Pavia (1329) shares claims between the Bavarian and Palatine lines.
Sponsalia at Hainburg: Leopold III's son William betrothed to Hedwig, daughter of Louis I.
Habsburg took Gorizian Istria and the Windic March on Albert III of Gorizia's death (1374); inheritance links with Count Meinhard VI continue.
Sigismund, Charles IV's son, is betrothed to Mary, heiress of Louis I.
Defensive alliance between Bern and the imperial city of Solothurn.
Burgrecht between Bern and Habsburg Fribourg.
Member of the Swabian City League of 4 Jul 1376 and its leading city; the league is banned at Eger in 1389.
Member of the Swabian City League of 4 Jul 1376; the league is banned at Eger in 1389.
Member of the Swabian City League of 4 Jul 1376; the league is banned at Eger in 1389.

facts.explanation: Richard II holds Edward III's claim to the French crown.
John of Gaunt, the king's uncle, styles himself King of Castile as husband of Constance, daughter of Peter I.
The Penthièvre (Blois) claim to Brittany, carried by Joan of Penthièvre.
John of Islay married Margaret, daughter of Robert Stewart (now Robert II).
Philip the Bold married Margaret of Male, heiress of Flanders, Artois, Nevers, Rethel and the County of Burgundy.
Arnaud-Amanieu VIII married Margaret of Bourbon.
Joanna I is Queen of Naples and Countess of Provence.
Richard II is King of England and Lord of Ireland.
The colony pays crown fees and black rent to Art Mór MacMurrough.
Black rent to the Midland lords for protection of the Pale borders.
English wool feeds the Flemish cloth towns through the Calais staple.
The Hanse trades from the London Steelyard under royal privileges.
The Infante John of Castile married Eleanor of Aragon (Peace of Almazán).
Charles of Navarre married Eleanor of Castile.
Ferdinand I claims Castile as Sancho IV's great-grandson against the Trastámara.
Peter IV claims Sicily after Frederick IV's death.
Peter IV claims the Catalan duchies of Athens and Neopatras; they accept him in 1379-80.
Genoese merchants run Granada's export trade (silk, sugar, fruit).
Regina della Scala, Bernabò's wife, claims the Scaliger inheritance.
Secondotto married Violante Visconti, Gian Galeazzo's sister.
Bernabò's daughter Viridis married Leopold III of Austria.
Bernabò's daughter Taddea married Stephen III of Bavaria.
Gambacorta's Pisa is Florence's port and partner.
Wenceslaus I is duke of Luxembourg in his own right and of Brabant through Joanna; the union ends on his death (1383).
Wenceslaus married Joanna of Bavaria-Straubing, Albert's daughter (d. 1386).
Frederick and Bernard of Brunswick married daughters of Elector Wenceslaus I.
The Welf sons of Magnus II claim Lüneburg under Welf house law.
Otto the Evil of Göttingen rules the Brunswick lands as guardian of Magnus II's sons under the 1370 pact.
Albert II claims the Danish crown for his grandson Albert IV, son of Ingeborg, daughter of Valdemar IV.
Empress Elizabeth, Sigismund's mother, is the daughter of Bogislaw V of Stolp.
Peace of Stralsund: free trade, toll rights and the Scanian castles held by the towns until 1385.
Bruges Kontor privileges after the 1358-60 blockade.
The Bergen Kontor.
The Peterhof Kontor.
Haakon VI married Margaret, daughter of Valdemar IV of Denmark.
Haakon VI, deposed in 1364, keeps the Swedish title; Olaf takes up the claim.
Sigismund of Luxembourg betrothed to Mary, heiress of Louis I; married 1385.
Through Sigismund's betrothal to Mary; Sigismund becomes King of Hungary in 1387.
Świdnica-Jawor: the dowager Agnes rules for life and the crown inherits on her death (through Anne of Świdnica, Wenceslaus's mother); falls in 1392.
William, son of Leopold III, betrothed to Hedwig (Jadwiga), daughter of Louis I, at Hainburg.
William's claim through Hedwig; ends with her marriage to Jogaila (1386).
Albert III married Beatrix, daughter of Burgrave Frederick V.
John II married Catherine of Gorizia.
German burghers dominate Stockholm and the towns; Lübeck carries Swedish copper and iron.
